view: Many authorities identify the chargers as horses, often warhorses running in God's cause; some describe the referent generally, while others specifically picture battle or raiding horses.
note: The horse reading is disputed by the camel reading; al-Ṭabarī prefers horses because he says camels do not make dabḥ.

view: A competing interpretation identifies the chargers as pilgrims' camels, especially the animals rushing from ʿArafāt through Muzdalifah toward Minā; some reports also mention camels at Badr or on a raid.
note: The camel interpretation is often tied to pilgrimage; some transmitters connect it with Badr, and one report has Ibn ʿAbbās withdraw his earlier horse answer.

view: Some notes leave room for more than one referent: horses and pilgrimage camels, horses in battle and pilgrimage, or either group as a valid object of the oath.
note: The dispute turns on whether the oath's descriptions point to warhorses, pilgrimage camels, or both; some authors say the wording accommodates both.

view: The oath may be understood more broadly as referring to swift runners, without limiting the referent to horses; one note explicitly allows horses, camels, or any running creatures.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr also notes proverbial human runners; Elmalılı includes any running creature.

view: Al-Qāshānī reads the chargers inwardly as striving souls traveling God's path through ascetic discipline, strenuous effort, and longing; their panting is longing's ardent exhalation.
note: This is an inward allegorical reading.

view: Al-Bayḍāwī's allegory makes the chargers souls that transmit holiness, kindle spiritual knowledge, attack caprice, raise desire for God, and enter the highest Garden.
note: The cited references are 83:18–19.

view: Several reports connect the horse reading with a delayed expedition against Banū Kinānah under al-Mundhir ibn ʿAmr: rumors said the force had died, then revelation announced its horses and progress to reassure the Prophet.
note: The accounts differ in details of the force, the delay, and how the report reached the Prophet; Ibn Kathīr calls one version very strange, and Ibn ʿĀshūr notes its weak chain.

view: An alternative occasion report places a late expedition in Tihāmah: Jewish and hypocritical onlookers worried people about missing relatives, then Gabriel explained that the horses had charged until they panted like foxes.
note: This is distinct from the Banū Kinānah account.

view: Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that the Prophet sent horses far away for a month without news, and the verse or surah was revealed during their absence.
note: The reports differ on whether they describe the whole surah or this verse's revelation.

view: A report links the surah to ʿAlī's campaign at Dhāt al-Salāsil after earlier commanders returned; another says the captives were bound in ropes like chains, and the Prophet recited the surah at dawn after Gabriel announced ʿAlī's victory.
note: The report is attributed to Abū ʿAbd Allāh and to Imams of the Prophet's household; some Sunni reports are also said to support it.

view: ʿAlī's camel argument invokes Badr: the Muslims had only one or two horses, so the oath cannot describe a large cavalry force; he instead identifies the chargers as camels, including pilgrims' mounts.
note: Some versions say two horses, others one or only al-Miqdād's horse; this is the main argument in the reported disagreement.

view: A report attributed to Ibn Masʿūd says the oath concerns the Hajj; the camel reading is also associated with pilgrims' movement between the rites.
note: Other reports name ʿAlī and additional authorities for this interpretation.

view: Ṣafiyyah bint ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib's verse pictures the pilgrims' chargers at Jamʿ raising dust, as poetic support for the camel interpretation.
note: The verse is cited as support for pilgrims' camels.

view: On the horse reading, ḍabḥ is the audible breath or panting of horses under exertion as they run; reports variously place the sound in the throat, chest, body, insides, or nostrils.
note: The descriptions vary over the precise location and quality of the sound; Ibn ʿAbbās also describes the horses lowering their lips as they prepare to race.

view: Horse ḍabḥ is distinguished from neighing or whinnying; some notes also distinguish it from roaring, barking, growling, a camel's bellow, and the sound made at food or a familiar owner.
note: One account proposes that forceful breathing kept muzzled horses from neighing and alerting an enemy.

view: Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to imitate the panting sound as “aḥ aḥ” or “aj aj”; another report gives the same imitation for camel ḍabḥ.
note: The notes vary between the spellings “aḥ aḥ” and “aj aj.”

view: On a camel reading, ḍabḥ may mean labored breathing or the driver's call; ʿAlī distinguishes horse panting from camel breathing.
note: This contrasts with explanations that derive camel ḍabḥ from ḍabʿ or treat it metaphorically.

view: Some camel interpreters explain ḍabḥ as ḍabʿ: extending or stretching the forelegs while moving, with ḥ substituted for ʿayn or the two words treated as equivalent.
note: Al-Zamakhsharī calls one explanation insecure; al-Kashshāf rejects the proposed letter interchange, while al-Qāmūs adopts it.

view: A broader lexical account says ḍabḥ can describe horses, dogs, foxes, and other animals; some authorities extend it to snakes, owls, hares, echoes, camels, and even a bow.
note: Some authors question the report restricting the sound to horses and dogs because Arabic usage is broader.

view: Some lexicographers say ḍabḥ originally described foxes and was transferred metaphorically to horses; they connect it with fire slightly changing or darkening a color.
note: The origin account accompanies broader usage, including foxes and horses.

view: Ḍabḥ is described as a rattling sound in the saddlebag or a movement of the horses' lips while they run.
note: These are additional proposed explanations of the sound.

view: Animals may pant from exhaustion, fear, or desire; one account relates the word to a change in their condition.
note: The named animals vary across reports.

view: Al-Zamakhsharī says that if the report from ʿAlī is authentic, ḍabḥ is borrowed metaphorically for camels as bodily terms are borrowed for people.
note: This preserves the camel reading while explaining the horse-associated word.

view: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says horsemen can be called al-ʿādiyāt, but ḍabḥ identifies horses themselves because it is their breathing sound when they run fast.
note: This distinguishes the referent of the participle from the sound attributed to it.

view: Al-Qurṭubī notes that ḍabḥ can also denote ash.
note: This is an additional lexical sense.

view: Al-ʿādiyāt is parsed as the feminine plural active participle of running quickly; the feminine form agrees with a non-rational referent, and the initial wāw is commonly taken as an oath particle governing the genitive.
note: Elmalılı and Ibn ʿĀshūr also discuss the root and form of al-ʿādiyāt.

view: The root ʿ-d-w is explained through crossing or exceeding a limit; its derivatives can express running, enmity, injustice, or spatial contagion, and the battle term ʿādiya can name troops that rush to attack.
note: Some restrict ʿadī to attacking infantry and ʿādiya to attacking cavalry.

view: Ḍabḥan is commonly analyzed as a cognate accusative, often with an implied verb meaning “they pant”; it can also be treated as a verbal noun or an adjective-like description of the runners.
note: Other parses treat it as a circumstantial accusative, or as governed by an implied verb; the notes preserve those alternatives below.

view: Other grammatical analyses make ḍabḥan a circumstantial accusative or verbal noun, supply an omitted verb, or treat it as a temporal adverb.
note: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ prefers the unrestricted verbal noun; Ibn ʿĀshūr gives a sound or manner-of-running analysis on the camel reading.

view: Al-Zamakhsharī allows ḍabḥan to govern or modify al-ʿādiyāt as if the phrase meant “panting runners”; Abū Ḥayyān objects that running and panting are not identical, and al-Samīn says the objection misreads the explanation.
note: The disagreement concerns the syntax and whether the phrase makes running synonymous with panting.

view: One parsing identifies al-ʿādiyāt with al-ḍābiḥāt because panting accompanies running; another note supplies the sound of the horses' insides with the implied verb that they pant.
note: These are additional lexical and grammatical formulations of the relation between running and panting.

view: A further reading makes the fāʾ between the chargers and the spark-making horses indicate that sparks result from hard running as hooves strike stones.
note: The notes connect the successive clauses to an ordered sequence of actions.

view: The expression ashabat is explained as traveling far across wide open plains, with sahb as the singular of suhūb for broad land.
note: This is a lexical explanation in the expedition report.

view: The common reading treats the opening wāw as an oath; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the oath convention magnifies its object and encourages far-fetched restrictions to warhorses or pilgrimage camels.
note: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ leaves the dispute unresolved and suggests the wāw may have moved beyond its literal oath function for a rhetorical purpose.

view: Because the following clauses depict an imaginary parable, Asad prefers translating the opening wāw as “Oh” instead of “By” or his usual “Consider.”
note: This is a distinct translation choice for the opening particle.

view: Al-ʿĀdiyāt names the surah in some early codices and commentaries without an opening wāw; other tafsirs retain the wāw in the title.
note: This note concerns the surah's title form.

view: The surah is classified as Meccan in several reports and as Medinan in others; the horse interpretation and delayed-expedition reports are sometimes used to support a Medinan date, while stylistic similarity supports a Meccan date.
note: The reports disagree on dating; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the Medinan view stronger despite noting a weak chain in one expedition report.

view: The surah has eleven verses.
note: Qutb also describes its rapid, forceful progression.

view: Jābir ibn Zayd places the surah fourteenth in revelation order, after al-ʿAṣr and before al-Kawthar.
note: This order accompanies the Meccan classification.

view: The surah's charging cavalry opening moves through a rapid sequence of attack images; its rough, rumbling rhythm mirrors the dust and the later disclosure of graves and hearts, framing the moral and resurrection scenes.
note: The image and frame are said to mirror each other; verses 6–8 discuss ingratitude and verses 9–11 judgment and disclosure.

view: Al-Biqāʿī reads the surah after al-Zalzalah as tracing the disposition behind evil deeds and imagined worldly gain, rebuking people who neglect Judgment, prefer worldly life, and fail to thank God.
note: He says the title fits because the oath and its answer point to the surah's purpose.

view: The oath by horses serves as evidence for the later claim that people are ungrateful to their Lord; their exhausted obedience contrasts with human ingratitude.
note: Islāḥī links the horses' exertion to dutiful service of their master.

view: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the surah recalls human ingratitude and love of wealth, which people know and which will be evidence against them at Judgment.
note: This is the surah's moral and eschatological message.

view: The oath recognizes horses' worldly and religious benefits: they can bring honor, wealth, protection, pursuit, escape, attack, and retreat, and can earn reward when used for God or sin when used for pride and harm.
note: Ibn al-Qayyim says the oath need not be limited to raiders; Muḥammad ʿAbduh reads it as encouragement to value, acquire, train, ride, and prepare horses for defense.

view: Al-Rāzī relates the oath to the benefits of camels in 88:17, contrasts human rebellion with God's service to people, and links it to pilgrimage; neglecting required Hajj is characterized as disbelief.
note: The cited verses are 88:17 and 3:97.

view: One transmitted saying calls failure to recognize the sanctity of a warrior's horse a branch of hypocrisy.
note: This is a separate ethical report about the horse.

view: Al-Biqāʿī says reflection on horses' distinctive features points to their being bestowed by one sovereign agent, so the oath is ultimately by God.
note: This is his theological explanation of the oath.

view: Ibn ʿĀshūr says that if the oath concerns pilgrimage camels, it honors mounts whose service is esteemed by both pagans and Muslims.
note: This explains why the camel reading could address both communities.

view: Ibn al-ʿArabī describes God as swearing by Muḥammad in Yā Sīn, by his life in al-Ḥijr, and here by his cavalry, including its neighing, dust, and sparks.
note: The cited passages are 36:1–2 and 15:72.

view: The basmala presents God as sovereign over all affairs, generous in creating and explaining, and specially merciful through guidance to devoted servants.
note: This is a theological reflection accompanying the surah commentary.

view: The verse about horses, mules, and donkeys says they are for riding and adornment, but al-Rāzī argues its purpose marker applies to riding rather than ornament.
note: The cited verse is 16:8.

view: Al-Qushayrī describes the basmala as a jealous word fit for a tongue protected from idle talk and backbiting and a guarded heart; only a spirit protected from attachments and veils is fit to love it.
note: These are devotional reflections accompanying the commentary.

view: A report promises ten good deeds for reciting al-ʿĀdiyāt for every person who spent the night at Muzdalifah and witnessed Jamʿ.
note: The report appears in more than one source.

view: A report attributed to Ubayy and raised to the Prophet measures a recitation reward by the number of people spending the night at Muzdalifah and witnessing Jamʿ.
note: This wording does not specify ten deeds.

view: Reports say al-Zalzalah and al-ʿĀdiyāt each equal half the Qur'an; another report assigns half to the two surahs together, a third to al-Ikhlāṣ, and a quarter to al-Kāfirūn.
note: The transmitted wordings differ on how the half-Qur'an reward is distributed.

view: Elmalılı extends the image to fire-sparking weapons and, by extension, fast motorized assault vehicles; he says a Meccan date would make this future reference especially clear and sees the plural forms and successive fāʾs as an ordered development of attack vehicles.
note: This modern application is Elmalılı's own extension.

view: Poetry is cited for the horse reading and for ḍabḥ as equine panting, including verses about charging horses and horses struggling in the pools of death.
note: The verses are offered as lexical evidence, not as separate referent interpretations.

view: Al-Naḥḥās notes that scholars disagree whether the chargers are horses or camels.
note: This records the dispute without preferring either interpretation.

view: Al-Māwardī cites a line about a horse at the charge for the horse interpretation and a poem by Ṣafiyyah about animals at Jamʿ for the camel interpretation.
note: The cited poetry supports the two competing referents.

view: Linguists describe the word's use for horses at the charge and compare it with poetic usage of horses in Iraq; another line describes blood-soaked chargers with necks like sacrificial stones.
note: The notes provide poetic support for the horse sense.

view: Al-ʿādiyāt derives from running or racing quickly; in battle usage ʿadī and ʿādiya can name troops that habitually rush to attack.
note: The root is also discussed through meanings of exceeding, hostility, and transgression above.

view: In one expedition account, the horses snort through their nostrils, spark with their hooves on stones, attack at dawn, raise dust, and reach the enemy together.
note: These actions describe the reported cavalry expedition.

view: Some say either a horse or a dog makes ḍabḥ while running.
note: This is one account of which animals make the sound.

view: Ibn ʿĀshūr says the surah condemns traits leading to loss in the afterlife, especially common among pagans and hypocrites, and warns Muslims against them.
note: This is his statement of the surah's admonition.
